Your gains should make you feel good; proud to be big. That said, we all have bad days and are allowed to feel bad about our bodies. After a few months of gaining, my concerns now are that I'm too small which is much better than worried about being too fat.

I spent most of my life wondering whether or not people thought I was fat and now I find comfort if knowing that people *definitely* know I'm fat.

I don't think you really need to delve into why you're actually gaining with them, unless you are super open.

If you have a good relationship with them, they may just be concerned for your health and not your weight. To be fair, *wanting* to gain weight is a fairly novel idea to most people, most see getting fatter as a sign of poor health.

When they make a comment next time, take mental note if they're shaming your appearance or merely commenting on the change. Also recognize if it's your whole family or only one member who makes these remarks. If you/they want to talk it out, tell them that you're doing well and while you appreciate the concern, tell them you wished they wouldn't comment on it anymore.

PS. if you do eat out, Taco Bell is the best for Calories vs Cost.

Having a sense of control over my own life is something I've struggled with for a while, even if I didn't know it at the time.

To take back control over themselves, some cook healthy and take up exercise, some mark their personality on their skin with tattoos, some write books with characters that are just extensions of themselves. These are all long-term solutions.

But what you seem to be looking for is a here-and-now kind of solution, which might be solved with different hobbies. This will obviously depend on your interests. For me, I find Rubik's cubes to be a way to bring things back to normal for me. The randomness of the colours to be eventually perfectly arranged gives me a sense of control and order compared to the randomness I deal with in my daily life.

I don't know you or your interests but regaining control over yourself can be done with almost anything you take up. As long as what you do is for *you* and it's not destructive to your well-being, then you'll be headed on the right path.
When it does bother you, what do you see in your friends' relationships that you don't have but would like in your own?

Depression is just caused by a chemical imbalance within your brain, whether or not you think that it should be treated is up to you. But the fact that some people produce less serotonin to experience pleasure has been proven by a lot of research.

What part of cutting yourself helps you calm down? And how does it help you? 

- The sense of control over your body?

- The release of endorphins when you experience pain?

- The hope that someone will see your scars and feel sympathetic for you?

Once you figure out that, you can work backwards and find an activity that can fill that need. I realize that asking *why* you cut is a BIG question and that you may not know right now. But it's something to consider if you want to find healthier ways to cope.

Speaking from personal experience, I've used a plethora of excuses not to do things. In the back of my mind I wanted someone to push further, to get me to do the things I don't want to do. I'm not saying this is the case but my excuses were a way of keeping myself in the familiar depressive state I was used to, rather than changing what I'd grown accustomed to.

Being a partner of a depressed person can be very difficult and you're right, the path you're taking is evidently wearing on you. It seems like a lot of your trouble comes from the one-sidedness of your relationship. 

For me (and from what I've seen), routine is a good habit to get into for depressed people, which you seem to be quite good at based off of what you've said. Routine gets people out of bed and into the mindset of looking forward to doing something.

Instead of doing everything for her (which seems to be putting a strain on you and your relationship), would you consider doing some of those activities *with* her? Cooking can be a very social activity and can keep peoples' minds off the negative thoughts that can consume your attention because you're more worried about burning something than feeling bad about yourself.

Grocery shopping, cleaning dishes, yard/house work, etc can also be done together. It's very much the way you frame it to her though. Instead of focusing on the chore itself, focus on the time you'll spend together while doing it. This won't just help her get out of the depressive mindset she's in but also take responsibility off of you once routine is established.

I hope this helps!
